# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–18 (Complete – Updated 134)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of fifth year** (Chapter 18). Spring 1816 events completed. Winter 1815-16 passed. Waterloo campaign: 16 June 1815 morning—regiment receives marching orders; by dawn 17 June—wounded return; 18 June (Sunday)—religious services. **Critical event (26 March 1816)**: Rebecca delivers son (Rawdon minor) and heir to Rawdon. **Spring 1816**: Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton; moves into Miss Crawley's house. Lady Southdown assumes control. Miss Crawley dies (spring/early summer 1816). **Late autumn 1815**: Mr. Osborne announces trip to Belgium; church incident with George's monument; confrontation with Colonel Dobbin in Brussels. **Chapter 17 timeline**: Approximately 3-4 years after Paris establishment; Rawdon and Rebecca now in Curzon Street, May Fair, London. **Chapter 17-18 events**: Pitt receives Rebecca's letter (graciously); declines to send £30,000 to Rawdon but offers hand and willingness to serve young Rawdon; nearly reconciliation between brothers. Pitt and Lady Jane absent from London when Rebecca arrives; Miss Crawley's house in Park Lane not yet occupied; Miss Crawley's domestics dismissed with gratuities; French novels sold to bookseller on Bond Street. Engaging society figures: young Lord Southdown, Lord Steyne. **Chapter 18 setting**: Summer, fifth year; river crossing at Quenwick, Gulton mentioned.
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham, Park Lane, Bond Street, Bayswater, Hyde Park, opera, Knightsbridge, nursery, parlour, ring), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calais, Dunkirk, Red Lion Square, Cursitor Street, Tooting, Gulton, Quenwick, Queen's Crawley, Clapham, Sugar-cane Lodge, Miremere, Valenciennes, Kensington Gardens, various other towns.

## Main Characters

**Colonel William Dobbin (now Colonel)**
- **Promoted to Major, then Colonel** after second Major's death at Waterloo. Greatly respected. Secret, unrequited adoration of Amelia. **Late autumn 1815**: In Brussels with recovering regiment. **Confrontation with Mr. Osborne**: Pleaded for forgiveness of Amelia and unborn child; complete rejection. **Role**: Brought Amelia back to England to her mother's house in Fulham. **Godfather to Georgy**: Became godfather of infant; purchases gifts constantly. **Chapter 17 status**: Visits Amelia's house daily; experienced crushing realization of hopeless love. Knows no place for him in her heart. Gently bears his fate; content to remain. **Chapter 18**: Cab described as "always hankering about her premises."

**George Osborne**
- **DEAD at Waterloo (16 June 1815, though monument inscription states 18 June)**. Married Amelia late April without father's consent; disinherited. Received £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. At Brussels: desperate flirtation with Rebecca. **Written final letter before daybreak 16 June** to father (delivered July): farewell before great battle; imploration for Amelia's provision; contrition; thanks. Seal robbed from dead body. **Monument erected** with inscription stating death 18 June, aged 28, "while fighting for his king and country." **Chapter 18**: Corporal Clink wears Waterloo medal; old gentleman (little George's grandpapa) holds boy and mentions "Captain George Osborne" of regiment—"died the death of a hero, sir, fighting against the Corsican tyrant." Colonel Rawdon blushes and confirms knowing him and his wife well.

**Amelia Osborne**
- **Widow and Mother**. Delivered infant Georgy, godchild to Colonel Dobbin. Status: receives £100/year widow's allowance; holds £2,000 in 4 percent annuities. **Health**: Severely shaken at Waterloo; recovery underway by time Dobbin brought her to England. **Chapter 17 status**: Living with parents in Fulham; fully recovered and devoted entirely to mothering Georgy. Existence is maternal caress; nurtures, dresses, lives upon him. Shows bright maternal pleasure. Laughs when Major arrives; kisses him with hopeless kindness. **Chapter 18 status**: **Maternal authority conflict with Mrs. Sedley**: One evening, Amelia discovered mother administering Daffy's Elixir (medicinal liquid) to sleeping infant without permission. Amelia, "gentlest and sweetest of everyday mortals," thrilled and trembled with anger at meddling with maternal authority. Cheeks flushed red (as when twelve years old). Seized baby from mother's arms, grasped at bottle, left old lady gaping, furious, holding guilty tea-spoon. **Coolness and secret jealousy** exist between mother and daughter regarding the boy. **Sunday outings**: Father (old Sedley) takes Georgy to parks and Kensington Gardens on Sundays (business prevents weekdays). Georgy loves redcoats; grandfather tells him of father's fame and introduces him to sergeants with Waterloo medals, pompously presenting child as "son of Captain Osborne of the --th, who died gloriously on the glorious eighteenth." Grandfather initially spoiled boy with apples and sweets until Amelia demanded solemn promise not to give child cakes, lollipops, or stall produce.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley**
- **Married to Rebecca**. Made last dispositions before campaign. Gallantry mentioned in Gazette; promoted to Lieutenant-Colonel; awarded C.B. **Paris period (3-4 years post-Waterloo)**: Quitted Guards and sold out. Lived comfortably on "nothing per annum" through gambling and financial ingenuity. **Incident with Colonel O'Dowd**: Violent fracas at Cafe de Paris; nearly challenged; Commander-in-Chief intervened; no duel. **Recent assessment**: Rebecca convinced him gambling income precarious. **Upon Miss Crawley's death news**: Hastily departed Paris; diverted to Dunkirk; owed more money at London than Paris. **Chapter 17-18 status**: Arranging inheritance affairs in London; wife and child followed; occupying furnished Curzon Street, May Fair house without payment. **Chapter 18 character and relationship with wife**: Fond of Rebecca; she always perfectly good-humoured and kind; she shows little scorn, perhaps likes him better for being fool. He is her upper servant and maitre d'hotel—goes on errands, obeys orders, drives in ring without repining, takes her to opera, fetches her punctually after solacing himself at club. Would like her fonder of boy but reconciles himself. "She's so clever, and I'm not literary and that." Requires no great wisdom to win at cards and billiards; makes no pretensions to other skill. **Wife encourages him to dine abroad**: "Don't stay and stupefy yourself at home to-night, my dear...some men are coming who will only bore you...now I have a sheep-dog, I need not be afraid to be alone." When companion came, his domestic duties became very light. **Love for son**: Has "great secret tenderness" for little Rawdon; takes him mornings to stables and park; doesn't escape Rebecca though she doesn't talk of it; doesn't annoy her but increases her scorn for him. Feels ashamed of paternal softness, hides from wife, indulges only when alone with boy. **Park incident (Chapter 18)**: Takes little Rawdon on pony (gift from Little Lord Southdown—black Shetland, "not much bigger than a large rat") for morning walks in park. Pleased to see old quarters and fellow-guardsmen at Knightsbridge; began thinking of bachelorhood with regret. Old troopers recognize ancient officer, dandle little colonel. Finds dining at mess and with brother-officers very pleasant. Says "Hang it, I ain't clever enough for her--I know it. She won't miss me"—and is right; wife does not miss him. **Story told at clubs and mess**: When recently threw son up violently and accidentally hit child's skull against ceiling, boy looked hard and piteous way, bit lips, clenched hands, didn't cry—said "For God's sake, Rawdy, don't wake Mamma." Rawdon tells story everywhere: "By Gad, sir, what a good plucked one that boy of mine is--what a trump he is! I half-sent his head through the ceiling, by Gad, and he wouldn't cry for fear of disturbing his mother." **Encounter in park (Chapter 18)**: Meets Corporal Clink of regiment with old gentleman holding boy about Georgy's age examining Waterloo medal. Gentleman says "He was a Captain in the --th regiment...Captain George Osborne, sir--perhaps you knew him. He died the death of a hero, sir, fighting against the Corsican tyrant." Rawdon blushes quite red, confirms: "I knew him very well, sir, and his wife, his dear little wife, sir--how is she?"

**Little Rawdon (Son)**
- **Born 26 March 1816**. In Paris: placed out at nurse in village with foster-brothers; nearly drowned on Calais sands through maid's neglect. **London period (Chapter 17-18)**: **Hidden upstairs in garret or kitchen**, scarcely noticed by mother. Passed days with French bonne; when Frenchwoman departed, taken to housemaid's bed in garret by compassionate servant. **Relationship with father**: Rawdon affectionate and devoted. Maintains private interviews every morning during shaving; boy sits on box watching with pleasure; sweetmeats hidden in old epaulet box. Father buys picture-books, cramming nursery with toys; walls covered with pictures father purchased and pasted. When off duty, spends hours with boy who rides on chest, pulls mustachios as driving-reins, spends days in indefatigable gambols. **Pony gift**: Little Lord Southdown bought black Shetland pony "not much bigger than a large rat" for boy. Father pleased to mount him and walk by side in park. **Chapter 18**: Takes accustomed morning walks in park with father and pony.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)**
- **Paris period (3-4 years post-Waterloo)**: Flourished; merits place of honour in Vanity Fair through wit, talent, energy. **By 26 March 1816**: Delivered son and heir. Wrote letters to Miss Crawley (attributed to Rawdon); sent war relics. **Miss Crawley's discovery and fury**: When fraud discovered, fury "beyond bounds"; repudiated as "most artful and dangerous person." **Parisian society success**: Achieved very smart and leading position; welcomed at distinguished houses. **Child care**: After amiable French custom, placed son out at nurse; did not care to visit; once infant spoiled dove-coloured pelisse; preferred nurse's caresses to mamma's. **Chapter 17-18 status**: **Negotiated creditor debts (COMPLETED)**: Offered creditors ninepence or shilling per pound dividend over fifteen hundred pounds to cover debts exceeding fifteen thousand pounds. Returned reporting "entire liberation." **London society reception**: Speedily became vogue among certain class; demure chariots at door with great people; opera box crowded; wit and cleverness made her fashionable. **Female society rejection**: Ladies hold aloof; doors shut; cut publicly by former friends. Now attends church regularly with Rawdon, carrying gilt prayer-books. **Letter to Pitt**: Composed gracious letter received by Pitt more graciously than previous compositions; Lady Jane so charmed expected instant division of aunt's legacy. **Pitt's response**: Declined £30,000 cheque but made handsome offer of hand; thanked Rebecca; pronounced willingness to serve little boy. **Chapter 18**: **Attitude toward son's crying**: When little Rawdon cries overhead from garret, dismisses sardonically; tells Lord Steyne "he'll cry himself to sleep"; did not offer to visit child. **Scorn for husband**: Secret tenderness for boy in husband's heart doesn't escape her though she doesn't talk of it; doesn't annoy her but increases her scorn for him. Fond of husband; always perfectly good-humoured and kind; perhaps likes him better for being fool. He is her upper servant and maitre d'hotel. Did not show scorn much. **Social activities**: Displays herself at gatherings (fresh pink dress, dazzling white arms and shoulders, thin hazy scarf, curls round neck, prettiest little foot in sandal and finest silk stocking). Sings charming French songs, plays piano, charms with wit. **Encourages husband's absence**: Tells him "Don't stay and stupefy yourself at home to-night, my dear...Some men are coming who will only bore you. I would not ask them, but you know it's for your good, and now I have a sheep-dog, I need not be afraid to be alone."

**Jos Sedley**
- **Chapter 18 status**: Bills for unlucky horses purchased—paid without question by him and agents. Never alluded to bargain; nobody knows for certainty what became of horses or how rid of them. **Isidor, Belgian servant**: Sold grey horse very like one Jos rode at Valenciennes sometime during autumn 1815.

**Mr. and Mrs. Sedley**
- **Mrs. Sedley**: Lacking energy; content to lie on shore where fortune stranded her; career of old couple is over. Could have taken in boarders after husband's ruin but had not spirit to bustle for "a few select inmates to join a cheerful musical family." **Mr. Sedley (Old Sedley)**: **Sunday pleasure (Chapter 18)**: On Sundays (business prevents weekdays), delights to take little grandson Georgy to neighbouring parks or Kensington Gardens to see soldiers or feed ducks. Georgy loves redcoats; grandfather tells how father famous soldier, introduces him to many sergeants and others with Waterloo medals, pompously presenting child as "son of Captain Osborne of the --th, who died gloriously on the glorious eighteenth." Treated some non-commissioned gentlemen to glass of porter. In first Sunday walks, disposed to spoil little Georgy, gorging boy with apples and sweets to detriment of health—until Amelia declared George should never go out unless grandfather promised solemnly not to give child cakes, lollipops, or stall produce.

**Other Characters**
- **Pitt Crawley and Lady Jane**: Married spring 1816 at Brighton. Moved into Miss Crawley's house. Inherited substantial legacy upon her death. Not in London when Rebecca arrived; made only one appearance to conduct business with lawyers and sell Miss Crawley's French novels.
- **Corporal Clink**: Of regiment; encountered in park with old gentleman holding boy about Georgy's age.
- **Little Lord Southdown**: Best-natured of men; main occupation buying knick-knacks to give away. Bought little Rawdon black Shetland pony "not much bigger than a large rat."
- **Lord Steyne**: Attends Rebecca's gatherings; sometimes plays ecarte with Rawdon; sits nodding over her piano singing. Rebecca tells him of little Rawdon's crying.
- **Mr. Raggles**: Loves and adores Crawley family. Supplies greengroceries; unpaid debts accumulate.
- **Other established characters**: Mr. Osborne (Elder), Mrs. O'Dowd, Sir William Dobbin, Mr. Clapp, etc.

## Critical Facts and Status
- **George's Monument Discrepancy**: Inscription states 18 June 1815; actual death 16 June 1815.
- **Amelia's Complete Recovery and Maternal Devotion**: Fully recovered; devoted entirely to mothering Georgy. Maternal authority fiercely defended against mother's interference.
- **Dobbin's Hopeless Love**: Recognizes no place for him in Amelia's heart; cab "hankering about her premises."
- **Rebecca's London Ascendancy**: Fashionable among certain class; ladies' doors shut; attends church regularly; courted by powerful men like Lord Steyne; wife to indifferent husband, mother to neglected son.
- **Little Rawdon's Contradictory Status**: Neglected by mother, hidden in garret; deeply loved and involved in private devotions by father; objects of grandfather's Sunday attentions (Georgy) versus father's affectionate care (little Rawdon).
- **Rawdons' Financial Operation**: Live in furnished Curzon Street house without payment; accumulate substantial unpaid debts while maintaining fashionable appearance; living "elegantly on nothing a year."
- **Mrs. Sedley-Amelia Conflict**: Coolness and secret jealousy regarding Georgy; maternal authority fiercely protected by Amelia.
